The motion passed. General Public Comment The Chairman opened the floor for general public comments. Hearing none, the floor was closed. New Business (Case No. RZ-09-26-01) Karl Bracqbien – Rezoning Application (Second Workshop) Karl Bracqbien has applied to rezone a 12.5-acre portion of Madison County tax map 50-55 from Agricultural (A-1) to Residential, Limited (R-1). The purpose of the application is to increase the number of dwellings that may be placed on the parcel, and future subdivision rights. Planning Commission Workshop Meeting Minutes – 10/21/2026 Page 1 of 5 Nicholls - advised that no changes had been made to the application to rezone a recently subdivided 12.5-acre parcel on John Tucker Road from A-1 Agricultural to R-1 Residential Limited. The applicant provided conceptual plans showing potential five- and six-lot developments. Bracqbien - confirmed that the proposal remains unchanged and requested rezoning the 12.5acre parcel from A-1 to R-1 to allow development of 5 or 6 home sites. His preference is 6 sites, but current perc tests have only shown 4 potential drain field locations so far. Whitman – asked if the applicant has considered ADUs in his development of the sites. Bracqbien – stated that the houses are intended for long term rental, and that ADUs are not part of the plan. Nicholls - clarified that the request is for rezoning, not subdivision approval, and that future development would require Health Department approval, including adequate drainfield and reserve areas, which could limit lot configuration. In response to Snyder, Nicholls confirmed that the parcel is legally recorded but awaiting a tax map number, which he agreed to pursue before action is taken. Whitman - questioned the potential for six additional ADUs under R-1 zoning. Nicholls confirmed that ADUs would be permitted by right, subject to applicable requirements, while Wright clarified that ADUs increase dwelling density, not lot count. Elliott - asked whether Bracqbien would proffer to prohibit ADUs. Bracqbien - declined, citing septic limitations and the possibility of future ADU rights under A-1 zoning. Nicholls - clarified that subdivision rights under A-1 zoning are currently exhausted, with one additional division available in 2029 and two in 2036. Carpenter - noted that rezoning would allow smaller, potentially more affordable rental homes than the four homes currently permitted under A-1. Whitman - questioned whether the potential density of 12 dwellings, including ADUs, aligns with the Comprehensive Plan. Gore - supported the rezoning based on the Plan’s housing objectives. Carpenter - cited existing development along John Tucker Road as consistent with the density of this proposal. The Chairman opened the floor for general public comments. Hearing none, the floor was closed. (Case No. SU-09-26-01) Cindy and John Decowski – Special Use Permit (Second Workshop) Cindy and John Decowski have applied for a special use permit to convert an existing singlefamily dwelling into a two-family dwelling (duplex) on property identified as Madison County Tax Map 30-78. The property is located at 27 Duet Road, contains approximately 5.032 acres, and is zoned Agricultural (A-1). A two-family dwelling (duplex) may be permitted in the Agricultural (A-1) Zoning District by special use permit pursuant to Article 14-3 of the Madison County Zoning Ordinance. Nicholls - reported no changes and noted that the proposed duplex would accommodate family needs where an ADU is not permitted. Decowski - confirmed that the proposed duplex would accommodate family members, as an ADU is not currently permitted in A-1 zoning. The Chairman opened the floor for general public comments. Hearing none, the floor was closed. (Case No. ZOA-10-26-01) Accessory Dwelling Unit Ordinance Amendment (First Workshop) Planning Commission Workshop Meeting Minutes – 10/21/2026 Page 2 of 5 Changes to the Accessory Dwelling Unit Ordinance are being considered to permit accessory dwelling units in the Conservation (C-1) and Agricultural (A-1) zoning districts. Nicholls - presented GIS data identifying approximately 891 C-1 parcels under 20 acres, 4,088 A-1 parcels under six acres, and 171 split-zoned parcels potentially affected by expanding ADU provisions, clarifying that actual eligibility would depend on existing dwellings and site conditions. He stated that The Commission was asked to consider whether to permit ADUs in either or both districts (A-1 and C-1) and whether to apply the same standards as residential (R1, R-2 and R-3) districts or apply different standards. Cowan - opposed extending ADUs to A-1 and C-1, citing concerns about increased residential density and preserving the County’s rural character and existing acreage requirements. Whitman - asked whether ADUs could be used as short-term rentals under the proposed ordinance. Nicholls - clarified that the state-mandated ADU requirements only apply to R-1, R-2 and R-3, allowing the County to establish separate standards in A-1 and C-1, should ADUs be allowed, including restrictions on short-term rentals, requirements for setbacks, etc. if they wish to do so. Carpenter – pointed out growing pains in neighboring counties and suggested that perhaps allowing ADUs in A-1 and C-1 as an SUP, might be the better way to handle the potential impact. Nicholls – asked that if an SUP is considered for ADUs in A-1 and C-1, then the Planning Commission should consider under what conditions they would approve or deny the SUP application. Nicholls – will send out a draft document to the Commissioners that extends the existing residential ADU provisions to include A-1 and C-1. Commissioners are asked to submit proposed changes specific to A-1 and C-1 districts for staff to compile and review at the next workshop. The Chairman opened the floor for general public comments. Hearing none, the floor was closed. (Case No. ZOA-05-26-01) Sign Ordinance Repeal and Replacement (Sixth Workshop) At the September 2, 2026, joint meeting of the Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors, the Planning Commission tabled their efforts in modifying Article 12 of the zoning ordinance. The Board subsequently directed the Planning Commission to consider repealing the existing Article 12, and developing a replacement better suited for the County’s needs. Nicholls - reported receiving sign ordinance comments from six of eight Commissioners for review. He also noted Mr. Elliott’s preference for targeted amendments to the existing ordinance rather than a complete repeal and replacement. Comments received from the various Commissioners were read and discussed through the shared document included in the meeting packet. Language will be drafted to clarify that signs painted on buildings containing text, logos, or commercial advertising cannot be classified as artwork to circumvent sign regulations. It was agreed that language should be included stating that any future Dark Sky policies must be conformed to, in regard to illumination for signs. Wright - recommended allowing the Board of Supervisors to establish and amend policies governing election signage on County property rather than codifying specific restrictions. Members expressed support for this flexibility and discussed making such policies publicly available. The Chairman opened the floor to public comment. Hearing none, the floor was closed. A) CALL TO ORDER B) PLEDGE TO THE FLAG C) APPROVAL OF AGENDA Upon motion of Claudia Lundy, the Board voted unanimously to approve. James Jennings, Andy Hargrove, Claudia Lundy, David Brankley, Sterling Wilkinson, Tom Tanner, Brenda Blackwell, Kirk Gravitt, Dennis Spence voted 'aye'. D) APPROVAL OF MINUTES 2026-9-14 Board Minutes.pdf Upon motion of Brenda Blackwell, the Board voted unanimously to approve. James Jennings, Andy Hargrove, Claudia Lundy, David Brankley, Sterling Wilkinson, Tom Tanner, Brenda Blackwell, Kirk Gravitt, Dennis Spence voted 'aye'. E) PLANNING AND ZONING (LUCKY CARSON/JOSH TANNER) E.1) Public Hearing - Special Exception Permit Application by Laurie Pearson to construct 20 small short-term residencies and common space accessory buildings (Election District 1) Laurie Pearson presented a special exception application for "The Faireborough at Shiney Rock", a proposed cottage development at 77 Union Chapel Road. The project would utilize approximately 5–7 acres of the 95-acre property and feature small, earth-sheltered cottages for short-term rentals. Pearson explained that the proposed 20 units could be reduced based on the Board’s recommendations. She emphasized the project's compatibility with the County’s Comprehensive Plan, including preserving rural character, promoting agritourism, increasing tourism revenue, supporting local businesses, and creating employment opportunities. She also discussed proposed agricultural activities, community partnerships, and interest from potential visitors. Pearson thanked those who had visited the property and requested the Board’s consideration of the application. The public hearing was opened. Pat Charles of Clarksville spoke in support of Laurie Pearson’s special exception application. Charles highlighted her involvement in local businesses and community organizations and emphasized the project’s potential to promote tourism and economic growth in Mecklenburg County. She described the proposal as a unique opportunity that aligns with the County’s goals of 3 supporting business development and tourism. Charles encouraged the Board to give the application fair consideration. Jonathan Billings, a lifelong resident of the Shiny Rock community, spoke in opposition to the special exception application. He emphasized the area’s longstanding agricultural character and his efforts to preserve farmland and prevent further development. Billings stated that he had spoken with numerous community members and had not encountered anyone in support of the proposal. He urged the Board to deny the application to preserve the rural character of the community. Herbert Ramsey, an adjoining property owner, spoke in opposition to the special exception application. He expressed concerns regarding potential conflicts with existing agricultural operations, increased traffic on Union Chapel Road, impacts on local infrastructure, and preservation of the community’s rural character. He urged the Board to consider the effects the proposed development could have on surrounding properties and farming activities. Bradley Pearson spoke in support of the special exception application, emphasizing the project’s focus on agritourism and preserving the rural character of the area. He stated that the proposed cottages would blend into the surrounding landscape while providing agricultural experiences for visitors, promoting tourism, and supporting local businesses. Alyssa Meling of L&D Professionals, the project’s civil engineering firm, addressed the Board regarding the proposed development. She stated that the project would comply with County zoning requirements and applicable state regulations, including landscaping, parking, lighting, stormwater management, and erosion control. She also discussed property boundaries, proper permitting for septic systems and wells, and coordination with VDOT to address traffic and access concerns. The public hearing was closed. Upon motion of Tom Tanner, the Board voted unanimously to approve the Special Exception Permit Application by Laurie Pearson to construct 20 small, short-term rentals and common space accessory buildings. James Jennings, Claudia Lundy, David Brankley, Sterling Wilkinson, Tom Tanner, Brenda Blackwell, Dennis Spence voted 'aye'. Andy Hargrove and Kirk Gravitt voted ‘nay.’ E.2) Public Hearing - Consideration of a Battery Energy Storage Siting Agreement with Terraform Power for the Mitchell Energy Center (Election District 7) Siting Agreement Mecklenburg Energy County FINAL 09.28.26..pdf Tony Deyerle of Terraform Power presented a proposed battery energy storage project near Linhardt Drive and Fort Mitchell Road. The presentation outlined the project’s location, site layout, safety measures, and proposed siting agreement. The representative highlighted an estimated $6.8 million in County revenue over 20 years, including $2.9 million in development payments. It was clarified that approval of the siting agreement would not constitute project 4 approval, as rezoning and special exception permit applications would still require review and approval. Mr. Deyerle also discussed emergency response planning, environmental considerations, and decommissioning responsibilities. The public hearing was opened. Stephan Worthy of Clarksville addressed the Board regarding the proposed battery storage project. Drawing on his experience with electric cooperatives, he expressed concerns that the project would primarily benefit the utility company rather than local ratepayers. He acknowledged the potential value of battery storage, particularly when paired with solar energy, but encouraged the Board to carefully evaluate the project’s benefits and financial commitments before making a decision. Dennis Floyd, Business Manager for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 80, spoke in support of the proposed battery storage project. He emphasized its potential to improve power grid reliability, manage peak energy demand, and provide economic benefits. Floyd also highlighted advancements in battery safety, the project's limited land disturbance, and the employment and apprenticeship opportunities it could provide for local electrical workers. He encouraged the Board to support the project. Baxtor Dinghan, a representative of EnergyRight, an educational nonprofit based in Richmond, spoke in support of battery energy storage systems. He highlighted their ability to improve grid reliability, manage peak electricity demand, and support economic development while requiring relatively small amounts of land. He emphasized the importance of appropriate siting and local oversight to ensure compatibility with the County’s land use priorities. He concluded by offering EnergyRight as a resource to County officials, staff, and residents. Kathy Keel of Chase City spoke in opposition to the proposed battery storage project. She expressed concerns regarding the concentration of solar facilities, data centers, and other developments in the Chase City area, stating that previous projects had provided limited benefits to the community. She also raised concerns about environmental impacts, water resources, fire safety, and the project's long-term economic benefits. Keel urged the Board to carefully consider the potential effects on the community and its natural resources. Charles Jackson of Chase City spoke in opposition to the proposed battery storage project. He expressed concerns about the increasing concentration of data centers, solar farms, and battery storage facilities in the Chase City area. Jackson encouraged the Board to thoroughly research the project and carefully consider its potential impacts before making a decision. Carlos Davis of Chase City spoke in opposition to the proposed battery storage project. He expressed concerns regarding fire safety, environmental impacts, and the increasing concentration of industrial developments in the area. Davis emphasized the lack of retail businesses and economic opportunities in Chase City, stating that previous developments had provided little direct benefit to residents. He urged the Board to prioritize projects that would improve the community and quality of life for its citizens. 5 The public hearing was closed. Upon motion of James Jennings, the Board voted unanimously to continue consideration of a Battery Energy Storage Siting Agreement with Terraform Power for the Mitchell Energy Center until the Board's November 2, 2026, meeting. James Jennings, Andy Hargrove, Claudia Lundy, David Brankley, Sterling Wilkinson, Tom Tanner, Brenda Blackwell, Kirk Gravitt, Dennis Spence voted 'aye'. E.3) Public Hearing - To Consider Proposed Amendments to the Mecklenburg County Zoning Ordinance Rachel Falkenstein of Line and Grade presented proposed amendments to the County’s recently adopted Zoning Ordinance. The changes included reducing by-right building heights in certain residential districts, modifying accessory structure setbacks, clarifying special event permit requirements, and updating outdoor storage regulations. Additional revisions addressed variance validity periods, agricultural structure signage, and minor clerical corrections. Falkenstein stated that the Planning Commission had recommended approval of the proposed amendments. Tom Tanner requested an amendment to the proposed Zoning Ordinance changes to require food trucks to maintain a valid annual permit from the State Fire Marshal’s Office in addition to the required Health Department permit. He emphasized that both permits are necessary and requested that the language be included in the ordinance amendments. The public hearing was opened. There was no public input. The public hearing was closed. Upon motion of Tom Tanner, the Board voted unanimously to adopt the following resolution and the additional change to include requiring food trucks to maintain a valid annual permit from the State Fire Marshall's Office in addition to the required Health Department Permit. James Jennings, Andy Hargrove, Claudia Lundy, David Brankley, Sterling Wilkinson, Tom Tanner, Brenda Blackwell, Kirk Gravitt, Dennis Spence voted 'aye'. A Resolution to Adopt Additional Zoning Amendments Whereas, on May 11, 2026, the Mecklenburg County Board of Supervisors adopted a new Zoning Ordinance for Mecklenburg County, which became effective on July 1, 2026; Whereas, the Board also requested a zoning ordinance review session, which was held by the Board’s Legislative Committee on August 17, 2026, to evaluate the initial effectiveness of the new Ordinance, and to determine if any legislative corrections were necessary and prudent; Whereas, the Legislative Committee identified several desired modifications, additions, and technical corrections to the Zoning Ordinance; 6 Whereas, the Board of Supervisors referred these selected items to the Planning Commission for the Commission’s evaluation at its September session; Whereas, the Planning Commission recommended that the Board enact the attached amendments to “clarify and improve development standards in Mecklenburg County”; and Whereas, the amendments have been posted on Meck44.com and have been duly advertised in the September 30 and October 7 editions of the Mecklenburg Sun. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS FOR MECKLENBURG COUNTY THAT: 1. The attached amendments to the Mecklenburg County Zoning Ordinance are hereby adopted. 2. The amendments adopted by the first enactment shall be effective immediately. The Zoning Ordinance, as amended by this action, shall govern all Planning and Zoning applications considered by the Planning Commission on and after the Commission’s October 15, 2026, meeting as well as any applications made to the County’s Planning and Zoning Department for legislative, administrative, or ministerial approval as of the date of enactment. F) VDOT F.1) Deed of Dedication to VDOT on Highway 92 (Election District 2) Russell Slayton explained that the County had acquired several parcels of land for the construction of a deceleration lane along Highway 92 near Chase City. For Planning Commission Meeting On: November 19, 2026 Prepared By: - Chariot Medlin Suggested Action: information only Attachments: lucky presentation for november meeting..pptx 14 Planning Commission 102 Zoning 15 Origins of Zoning in the USA • 1916 Zoning Resolution New York City • Adopted to protect residents from skyscrapers blocking light and air • Introduced setbacks, height restrictions, and separating residential, industrial and commercial uses • The blueprint for modern zoning nationwide 16 Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. • Village of Euclid adopted a zoning ordinance • Property owned by Ambler Realty was zoned to prevent industrial uses • Ambler contended that the ZO reduced the value violating their rights to liberty and property under the due process and equal protection clauses of the 14th Amendment • The Supreme Court concluded that the speculative damages claimed by Ambler Realty were insufficient to invalidate an otherwise valid exercise of the village's police power. 17 What are Police Powers • The Tenth Amendment of the Constitution states “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” • Police powers are the fundamental ability of a government to enact laws to coerce its citizenry for the public good, although the term eludes an exact definition • The states have broad authority to regulate and is limited by the state and federal constitution 18 Important Supreme Court Cases • Buchanan v. Warley (1917) – race-based zoning violates the 14th Amendment • Nollan v. California Coastal Commission (1987) – the Essential Nexus test, there must be a nexus between legitimate state interests and conditions for a permit • Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Commission (1992) – total takings test, a taking occurs when regulation denies all economically beneficial or productive use of land • Doland v. City of Tigard (1994) – conditions of a permit must be proportional to the adverse impacts of a new development • Kelo v. City of New London (2005) – a government taking of property from one owner to another in the furtherance of economic development is a permissible public use under the 5th Amendment 19 Types of Zoning • Euclidean zoning – land use by type (residential, commercial, industrial) • Flat zoning – each use is only permitted in its corresponding zone • Hierarchical zoning – less intense uses are permitted in higher intensity zones. Pyramid structure • Form Based - land development regulation that fosters predictable built results and a walkable public realm by using physical form. Tells you how to build 20 Houston, Texas • Largest municipality in the USA without an adopted zoning ordinance • Population of 2.4 million • Development is governed by ordinance codes that address how property can be subdivided • The City codes do not address land use 21 Mecklenburg County P.O. She stated that the second budget supplement included carryover for federal funds, including Title funds and IDEA funds, as well as a grant and payment from the Virginia Department of Education. Supervisor Jessie made a motion to approve School Budget Supplements FY 202701 and FY 2027-02, which was seconded by Supervisor Bill Harris. The following roll call carried the motion: Supervisor Jessie – Aye; Supervisor Williams – Aye; Supervisor Bill Harris – Aye; Supervisor Crittenden – Aye; and Chairman Don Harris – Aye. Dr. Seitz also updated the Board regarding the high school gym. She stated that the school division was waiting on the insurance adjuster and appraiser for next steps and that she had contacted VaCorp to ask that the matter be moved forward due to the gym being used by both the school division and the community. The Board also discussed the high school drainage issue. Dr. Seitz stated that Dustin Harris, the school division’s operations director, met with Mr. Gentry and Mr. Chip England, County Engineer, to review plans from the 2002 high school renovation and a subsequent athletic complex addition. She stated that staff had been unable to locate civil engineering information showing whether drainage had been rerouted. The Board discussed continuing the investigation, including the possibility of inspecting the drainage system with a camera. EDA MARKETING: Report Only. CHESAPEAKE BAY PUBLIC ACCESS AUTHORITY PRESENTATION: Mr. Lewis Lawrence, with the Middle Peninsula Planning District Commission and the Middle Peninsula Chesapeake Bay Public Access Authority, addressed the Board regarding dredging and the development of a municipal dredging program. Mr. Lawrence stated that dredging is becoming a local government responsibility due to reduced federal involvement, which creates policy questions for localities regarding where to dredge, why to dredge, and how to determine what is in the public interest. Mr. Lawrence stated that dredging is an issue of greater than local concern and that jurisdictions across the Middle Peninsula are facing the same challenges. He discussed the importance of maintaining marine highways for the local economy, boating safety, the seafood industry, waterfront property values, and local tax revenue. He stated that Middlesex County has seven federal channels, the most of any locality in the Middle Peninsula, and that many shallow-water dredging projects are receiving little or no federal funding. Mr. Lawrence stated that one of the most difficult issues is not only dredging itself, but where dredged material will be placed. He explained that dredge-material placement sites and local cooperation agreements are critical and that the Corps of Engineers is moving away from recognizing certain easement placement areas. He stated that, absent a placement strategy, dredging projects may not be able to move forward or may become significantly more expensive. Mr. Lawrence discussed possible funding and organizational tools, including service districts, tax increment financing, sanitary districts, community development authorities, VRA loans, one-time grants, and public-private partnerships. He stated that service districts may provide local governments with flexibility and a predictable revenue stream for dredging needs, but each creek would need a revenue-generating strategy before moving forward. Mr. Lawrence stated that two legal documents are needed to activate participation in the municipal dredging program: an operating agreement and an operating program. He stated that the documents have been reviewed through the Virginia Port Authority and Sans Anderson and that participating jurisdictions would have a seat at the table and access to state funding. He stated that the County would need to determine whether to participate and which creeks or channels it may want included. The Board discussed staff workload and whether participation in a regional program would reduce the burden on County staff. Mr. Lawrence stated that the intent is for the Public Access Authority to serve as the agent on behalf of participating localities and to reduce the need for County staff to manage dredging projects directly, although certain federal cooperation documents may still require local government action. The Board also discussed how dredging priorities would be determined. Mr. Lawrence stated that prioritization is a local policy decision and could be based on federal channels, commercial activity, economic development, real estate value, public need, or other local considerations. He stated that public input and surveys may help identify where consistent dredging needs exist. Ms. Watson stated that she serves as the Community Network Builder for the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula through the Institute for Engagement and Negotiation at the University of Virginia. Ms. Watson stated that the proposed regional housing assessment would include all ten counties in the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula. She stated that the County was not being asked to provide funding, but was being asked to provide a letter of support and to cooperate with the data analysis, interviews, and community engagement needed for the assessment. Ms. Watson stated that the project is being funded by a $200,000 Virginia Housing grant, or approximately $20,000 per county. She stated that the assessment would include county-level, planning district-level, and full regional deliverables. She also stated that Virginia Tech would complete the data collection and Housing Forward Virginia would Back to Agenda 5 BOS Board Packet Page 7 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES October 6 , 2026 assist with the final analysis. The full process is expected to take approximately three years, with the main data portion expected to be completed within the first two years. Carl Schwendeman, 1727 Theresa Lane, asked about putting in a full turn lane now rather than later. He also mentioned putting in a sidewalk or trail with buffering. Keith Buch, 2246 Branch Forest Way, stated that Main Street Homes is preferred developer and mentioned the Mill Quarter area and stated support for the project. Mark Adams, 4365 Steiger Creek Drive, asked what the buffer between the creek and the houses would be, and stated that he supports the turn lane. Seeing no one else come forward, Chair Hughes closed the public hearing. Mr. Hatcher asked for clarification on the buffer the speaker mentioned. Mr. Clendening responded that it would be 100 feet and 25 feet for structures off that. Ms. Bowlin mentioned that the subdivision to the north was an average of five acres with a two-acre minimum. Mr. Hatcher discussed the context for traffic heading west on Route 60. Vice-Chair Hall discussed the number of trucks heading down the road and stated that a turn lane would be warranted in this case. Ms. Bowlin asked about the turn lane proffer. Mr. Deal stated that there is about 30 or 40 feet of width for a taper and will have enough width for a vehicle. He stated the issue is that VDOT will require 400’ length for a full turn lane and will not give a half of a turn lane. He stated that the number of vehicles from the new lots is low compared to the church next to them, and it is unlikely VDOT will warrant a turn lane. Mr. Hatcher stated that a ten-lot private road would not be required to do a turn lane and are prevalent in Powhatan. Ms. Bowlin mentioned that most of those are on rural roads and not on Route 60. Mr. Hatcher made a motion to recommend approval of Case 26-07-REZ-C with proffered conditions. 8 . Ms. Winall seconded. Hatcher, Winall, Bowlin AYE. Hughes, Hall NAY. December 3rd, 2026 Planning Commission Meeting ADJOURNMENT 600 North Main Street, Suite 107 | Woodstock, Virginia 22664 | 540-459-6185 https://www.shenandoahcountyva.gov/197/Planning-Commission MINUTES OF MEETING OF THE SHENANDOAH COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION October 1, 2026 A regular meeting of the Shenandoah County Planning Commission was held in the Board Meeting Room, 600 North Main Street, Woodstock, Virginia on October 1, 2026. The following members of the Planning Commission were present: Tommy Miller, Keith Stephens, Debbie Keller, James Fagan, Gary Lantz, Eunice Terndrup, and Supervisor Dennis Morris. The following members of the Board of Supervisors were present: Tim Taylor, David Ferguson, Mark Dotson, Steve Baker and Kyle Gutshall. Others present included Director of Community Development Lemuel Hancock, Zoning Administrator Brenna Menefee, County Planners McKenzie Allen and Jack Hurst, and Permit Technician, Summer Andes. An invocation was given, followed by the Pledge of Allegiance. Keith Stephens made a Motion, seconded by James Fagan, to approve the agenda, with an amendment to change Section 2, under Public Hearings; the 4th to last word should read yard instead of years. A vote of 7-0 approved the Motion as follows: Ayes: Miller, Stephens, Keller, Fagan, Lantz, Terndrup and Supervisor Morris. James Fagan made a Motion, seconded by Eunice Terndrup to approve August 27, 2026 minutes. A vote of 7-0 approved the Motion as follows: Ayes: Miller, Stephens, Keller, Fagan, Lantz, Terndrup and Supervisor Morris. Debbie Keller made a Motion, seconded by Eunice Terndrup to amend the September 3, 2026 minutes due to typographical errors discussed with staff. A vote of 7-0 approved the Motion as follows: Ayes: Miller, Stephens, Keller, Fagan, Lantz, Terndrup and Supervisor Morris. Supervisor Tim Taylor called the Board of Supervisors to order. REPORTS An update was given by Tumbling Run about the 2026 season. Two large rodeos were held; one in June, which sold out, and one in September, which sold about 1,200 tickets. Another rodeo was held for charity in July. 2027 Tumbling Run is planning two large rodeos and two for charity. Amy Dill and Lemuel Hancock gave a presentation about Capital Improvement Projects (CIP) for Fiscal Year 2028 – 2032. In September a Capital Planning Work Session was held, and some survey results were received from Planning Commission. They asked, moving forward into November, for a vote from PC to move forward to the Board of Supervisors for their Work Retreat and discussing the annual budget. Lemuel Hancock gave a presentation on ordinance reviews and updates: Decommissioning, Energy and Data Centers. He stated that currently, if an application is received, the standard fee level of $500 is used. He proposed to increase the application fees, for Data Center and Onsite Power Generation Facilities, at the November PC meeting. Any Third-Party review would be passed on to the applicant, and that would be included in the Building Code and Zoning Code fee schedules. Lemuel Hancock asked for a PC recommendation to have a public hearing about this. Keith Stephens asked if the fees being addressed were enough to cover the reviews for Data Centers and Onsite Power Generation Facilities. Lemuel Hancock answered that $5,000 was the previous high, and when staff checked with other communities, they found that they had Data Center specific fees, and they were five to six times higher. He felt the $5,000 would work for our area but stressed that currently the fee is only $500. Page 1 The PC gave an “All in Favor” vote to update the fee schedule for Data Centers and Onsite Power Generation Facilities and present at the November PC meeting. PUBLIC HEARINGS 1. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-01. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-4 of the County Code to revise the definition of “Garages, Public” to add that certain uses including, but not necessarily limited to, renting, selling, or storing motor vehicles, are “permitted as an accessory use only to a permitted public garage”. Brenna Menefee gave a presentation. She explained that the primary use of the business would have to be servicing, repairing or equipping motor vehicles. Then, as an accessory use, they could also rent, sell or store motor vehicles. 2. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-02. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-4 of the County Code to make certain amendments to the definition of “Inoperative Motor Vehicles”, which amendments include, but are not necessarily limited to, (i) clarifying that trailers or semi-trailers can be Inoperable Motor Vehicles, and (ii) providing that vehicles that do not have valid license plates and valid inspection decals, unless exempt, are Inoperable Motor Vehicles, and (iii) requiring that Inoperable Motor Vehicles shall not be parked or stored in the required front yard at any time. Brenna Menefee gave a presentation. James Fagan stated this was more of a prohibited use, rather than a definition. Tommy Miller agreed that this was not a definition. Keith Stephens stated that farmers use trailers for farming, and they may not have tags on them. Brenna Menefee stated that they would not be able to park them in the front yard, but if they were Farm Use, they would have proper things from DMV that would exempt them. Dennis Morris asked for clarification as to what exactly is allowed. He stated that Farm Use Vehicles can sometimes sit in the yard years. Brenna Menefee explained that this amendment would help to make things clearer. She told PC that staff pursues many issues where they end up in court. She stated that many times the complainant has an issue with the vehicles being parked near the road/front yard; telling the violator that they cannot have more than five vehicles, because that makes them a Vehicle Graveyard, does not satisfy that complainant, because many times there are not more than five vehicles, but they are by the road. Mark Dotson stated that a farmer can use a semi-trailer box as storage, with or without wheels, without Farm Use tags. Brenna Menefee explained that storage trailers on the ground are not considered vehicles, and currently code does not allow those containers to be set just anywhere. They have been allowed as accessory use, if they are screened appropriately and on ag land or industrial land; not subdivisions. Mark Dotson stated that after reading through our Zoning Code, he saw that we are missing several aspects of State Code that we reference with screening or shield of view. He explained that we do not want to have a negative impact on individuals that have valid uses for trailers, semi-trailers or vehicles that are currently being used. Brenna Menefee explained that she liked the verbiage of trailer and semi-trailer, because she is currently working on a violation with a right of way that is being blocked by a tractor trailer. People are having to drive around it just to get to their property. She stated that she cannot make the owner move the trailer, Page 2 but she is unwilling to drop the violation until it is moved, but she is unsure that a judge would agree with her, because the current definition does not state that the trailer cannot be there. John Price spoke against the proposed ZTA. He explained that sometimes people may not be able to fix a vehicle right away, but they do not have a place to store the vehicle while it is not operable. He felt that if the VDOT right of way is enforced, no other ordinance is needed. Josh Stevens stated that State Code pretty much says what we should do. He was concerned with the wording; it should be the same as what is used by the State. He explained that more specifics need to be given with how the code reads. He asked that three things be looked at: • • • Look at the word “and”, and how it relates to the existing State Statute Clarify, particularly with trailers that already have running gear removed, that are being used as stationary storage; does that automatically make that an inoperable vehicle Address vehicles and trailers that are truly exempt from state inspection 3. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-03. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-4 of the County Code to create a new definition for “Dwelling, Accessory Detached” that will replace the existing definition of “Dwelling, Accessory”. Brenna Menefee gave a presentation. She explained that currently, in all zoning districts, a primary and an accessory dwelling are allowed. This would still allow that, but it must remain under the same ownership. 4. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-04. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-4 of the County Code to create a new definition for “Dwelling, Accessory Attached”, which definition will also contain certain requirements and regulations that pertain to Accessory Attached Dwellings. Brenna Menefee gave a presentation. She explained that currently, in all zoning districts, a primary and an accessory dwelling are allowed. This would still allow that, but it must remain under the same ownership. 5. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-05. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-106 to revise certain standards and adopt new standards pertaining to the process for enforcement and revocation of special use permits. Lemuel Hancock gave a presentation. He explained that this would give a clear process of what would happen if a special use permit was violated. • Two or more violations in an 18-month period: The applicant or violator would receive a notice from the Zoning Administrator. After two of those are sent, then there will be a PC review, and possibly Board of Supervisor review John Price spoke against the ZTA proposal. He asked for more specifics on what would need to happen to make a violator more accountable. He stated that fees may not stop violators. Mr. Taylor adjourned the Board of Supervisors. Page 3 PUBLIC COMMENT NOT PREVIOUSLY, OR TO BE, DISCUSSED AS PART OF A PUBLIC HEARING Jess Estienne presented a petition she started against Special Use Permits in Fort Valley. She was concerned with light and noise pollution, wildlife safety, limited resources for rescue, traffic, roads and the historical value of the valley. OLD BUSINESS 1. Special Use Permit 26-09-01: A Special Use Permit pursuant to Section 165-11B(3)(t) of the County Code allowing a rural resort on 230.795 acres, more or less, on certain real property zoned C-1 Conservation, located at Narrow Path, Fort Valley (Tax Map No. 084A003, 072A002A, 072A002B, 07203003, 072A003B, 07203004, 07203001, 072A003A, 072A004A, 07SA004B, 07205003, 07205004, 072A018A, 072A018B, 072A020). The rural resort will consist of a retreat center and related accessory structures. Brenna Menefee gave a brief recap of the presentation, given September 3, for the proposed SUP. She explained that the applicant was offering a few additional conditions as follows: • • • • Limiting the number of events Maximum number of attendees Removing portable bathroom facilities from the property Event related lighting and amplified music to end at 10PM Lemuel Hancock stated that as of 3PM today, VDOT had replied that required site distance for the location was still not met. Kristie Rodriguez, applicant for the proposed SUP, spoke about the additional conditions that were being offered. James Fagan made the comment that the PC must make a motion tonight based on what is there now and the current information; not on what can be done or will be done. James Fagan also stated that the VDOT requirements are still not satisfied. Kristie Rodriguez said they would be willing to remove the existing sign. The applicant asked if the SUP could be tabled until the requirements were satisfied and then revisit to decide or make the SUP approval contingent on the requirements being met; giving the applicant time to finish the VDOT requirements. James Fagan said PC could not table the SUP. Tommy Miller said he did not think PC could make a decision with contingencies. Kristie Rodriguez then asked if she could table the SUP proposal until the VDOT work is done. Lemuel Hancock explained that without the applicant asking staff or putting it in writing to them, PC must make a decision. text: Staff Memorandum – Sign Modification Request Planning Commission – November 5, 2026 Applicant / Property Owner: Address of Subject Property: Tax Map Number: Spring Oak Bedford LLC / Bedford Residences LLC 931 Ashland Avenue 172-A-1-T, RPC 80500871 Lot Size: Existing Use: Existing Zoning District: Requested Change: 29.87 acres Nursing Home Low Density Residential, R-1 Sign Modification for Freestanding Signs The applicant is requesting modification to sign standards per Section 816.14 of the zoning ordinance in the Low Density Residential (R-1) zoning district for an existing nursing home use. The requested change is to allow a new, additional freestanding sign where only one freestanding sign can be permitted in the R-1 district per the zoning ordinance, and signs on existing columns. Background: The Spring Oak (former Elks Home) nursing home complex predates zoning and is designated Low Density Residential (R-1) zoning district. Signage in residential districts is limited with fewer restrictions on non-residential uses. Signs are regulated in residential zoning districts as follows (underlined provisions are relevant to this request): 816.09. Signs in Residential Zoning Districts. a. Individual residences located in zones R-1, R-2, R-3 shall not display additional signage beyond that permitted by section 816.03 of this Land Development Ordinance. b. Non-residential uses located in residential zones R-1, R-2, R-3 shall be permitted to display one wall or freestanding monument sign of up to 16 square feet. c. Only one sign shall be allowed per parcel. d. Pole mounted signs shall not be permitted. e. Illuminated signs shall not be permitted in residential zoning districts Ordinance Section 816.14 Modification: As state above, Zoning Ordinance Section 816.09 regulates signs in residential districts. At this non-residential use location, one freestanding monument sign of up to 16 square feet can be permitted. The applicant requests several modifications. The first request is to reface the existing “Elks National Home” pole sign from approximately 30 square feet of area to 91.5 square feet of area (written on the application), exceeding the 16 square feet. The area measurement from the sign image appears to be less than 91.5 square feet. The nonconforming pole sign structure would not change, however, the increase in area would be a modification. The nonconforming pole sign may be considered a vested nonconformity since that part of the nonconforming structure is not being modified. 1 The second request is to add a second freestanding sign to provide directional signage to emergency vehicles. This sign would be 12 square feet in area on a pole sign that is six feet tall. The placement is farther down Ashland from the first freestanding sign at a driveway. Although not listed in the letter, staff seeks action for a third part of the permit application to allow two new signs to be placed on the existing entry columns. The larger sign measuring 7.77 square feet could be considered directional for the emergency service direction and elevator location. The second is 6.22 square feet and facing the opposite travel direction. Planning Commission Action: Zoning Ordinance Section 816.14 allows an applicant to request a modification of the sign regulations: 816.14. Modification. Modification of the sign regulations found in this ordinance may be requested by application to the Planning Commission. The Planning Commission shall weigh the merits of the application and render a decision. A public hearing may be held if required by the Zoning Administrator. As the Zoning Administrator, I did not require a public hearing be held for this request with the nature of the requests. Precedent: The Planning Commission denied a request from Bedford Lutheran Church to modify several sign requirements in the R-1 district in favor of a monument style base and a possible change to B-2 for the constructed sign scale. Drawings showing the height, sign perimeter and area dimensions, means of support, method of illumination, landscaping, and design for the existing and proposed sign; e. A record plat plan or drawing showing dimensions of building and relationship of building and/or sign to adjacent property lines, sidewalks, streets, intersections and buildings; f. Any other information that the zoning administrator may request to ensure compliance with the provisions of this ordinance and other applicable town regulations; g. Name, mailing address and phone number of property owner. Property owner or legal representative must sign all signage applications. 816.15. Expiration of sign permits; extension. A sign permit shall expire and become null and void if the sign is not erected within a period of six months from the date of permit issuance. An application for one six month extension of the permit may be made to the zoning administrator by the permit holder prior to expiration of the original permit. An extension may only be granted when the proposed sign is in compliance with all current applicable regulations, and in no case shall a permit be valid for more than a total of 12 months without the authorized sign being erected. 816.16. Revocation of sign permit. The zoning administrator may revoke a permit or approval if it is found that there has been concealment or misrepresentation of material facts in either the application or plans. Furthermore, failure to adhere to the requirements of this ordinance in the construction and maintenance of a sign automatically cancels such permit, and said sign or structure shall be removed by the property owner forthwith. These regulations shall apply to the construction, erection, alteration, use, relocation or reconstruction of all signs placed for public observance within the Town of Bedford. I hereby certify that this application is complete and accurate to the best of my knowledge. For temporary signs, I certify the sign shall be removed by the specified time. Violation of the provisions of this application may result in enforcement action. By signing, I certify that I have read and understand the Regulations on pages 3 through 7 attached to the application. Councilmembers Present: Mayor Tina Gambill, Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle, Councilmember Jean Davis, Councilmember John Chinault, Councilmember David Storke, Councilmember Randy Hageman, Councilmember Jeff Voit Councilmembers Absent: Councilmember Dan Webb Staff Members Present: John Anzivino, Interim Town Manager/Clerk; Jeff Gore, Town Attorney; Justin Cecil, Bowling Green Police Chief; Vianne Baylor, Deputy Town Treasurer; Perry Hickman, Capital Projects & Grants Manager/Assistant Town Manager; Jeffrey Smith, Administrative Assistant/Deputy Clerk. Darla Odom, Deputy Zoning Administrator, participated remotely to discuss potentials for the location of retail cannabis facilities and their regulation under the Town’s zoning ordinance CALL TO ORDER AND ESTABLISHMENT OF QUORUM:  Six Councilmembers were present, Councilmember Dan Webb was absent, and a quorum was established. CONSENT AGENDA: 1. Minutes- September 3, 2026  Councilmember Jean Davis identified a correction under Member Comments. Councilmember Jeff Voit moved to approve the September 3, 2026, minutes as corrected. The motion was seconded by Councilmember Randy Hageman and carried unanimously by right-hand raise, with six members voting and one absent.  Councilmember David Storke mooved to add Item 13, Proposal for Services, to the agenda. The motion was seconded by Councilmember Randy Hageman and carried unanimously by right-hand raise, with six members voting and one absent. PUBLIC COMMENTS: 3 MINUTES PER INDIVIDUAL  None. MEMBER COMMENTS:  Councilmember Jeff Voit reported that the Town’s Clean Sweep event had lower participation than previous events but good walk-in attendance and positive feedback. He encouraged attendance at the October 17 Harvest Festival, the Music on the Green concert the preceding evening, and the upcoming Pirate Festival in Port Royal. 3 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 2 of 5 STAFF REPORTS & PRESENTATIONS: 2. Bowling Green Police Department Report, Chief Justin Cecil  Town Council received the Bowling Green Police Department report. Chief Justin Cecil advised that Harvest Festival preparations were proceeding smoothly. Mayor Tina Gambill thanked the department for its work to keep attendees safe. 3. Utilities Report, Inboden Environmental Services  Mark Inboden presented the utilities report. Monthly water production totaled approximately 4.3 million gallons, averaging approximately 141,000 gallons per day. Wastewater flow totaled approximately 4.12 million gallons, averaging approximately 133,000 gallons per day. Effluent monitoring results were within permit limits, and no operational issues were reported. 4. Public Works Department Monthly Report, Shawn Fortune, DPW  Town Council received the Public Works Department monthly report. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino advised that Public Works Director Shawn Fortune was absent due to illness and offered to address questions. No questions were presented. 5. Finance Director/Treasurer’s Report, Vianne Baylor, Deputy Town Treasurer  Vianne Baylor presented the finance report. Council discussed unpaid utility balances associated with apparently vacant residences and whether the $250 utility deposit adequately covered those balances. Staff was asked to review the deposit amount and outstanding balances for further consideration. 6. Capital Improvement Projects Presentation, Perry Hickman, Capital Projects & Grants Manager  Perry Hickman reviewed the well-replacement and Gross Alpha treatment project, estimated at approximately $8.2 million with approximately $59,000 in annual operating and maintenance costs. Approximately $6.2 million has been allocated through the Virginia General Assembly, with the balance anticipated through EPA funding coordinated by the Virginia Department of Health (VDH). He reported that the memorandum of agreement (with who? )had been signed September 3 and that Stantec’s engineering proposal and test-well specifications had been submitted to VDH. He also reviewed the approximately $1.1 million waterline replacement project associated with Congressman Vindman’s community project funding request, including approximately $746,000 in anticipated federal funds and a $358,962 Town match whose funding source remained to be determined. The project would serve portions of Main Street, Chase Street, and North Main Street near government facilities. The containerized sludge-dewatering equipment at the wastewater treatment plant was installed on September 24 and is operating successfully. Virginia Rural Water Association camera inspections were scheduled for October 8 to help identify inflow and infiltration in select sewer collection lines, with targeted smoke testing of lines also under consideration. Recent Main Street water-main repairs for two breaks cost approximately $29,000 and $18,200, and Council discussed the deteriorated pipe condition and need for additional replacement. Mr. Hickman also reported receipt of a $5,000 Dominion Energy grant for the BGVA Main Street mural and the anticipated transfer of those funds to BGVA Main Street. No motion concerning the mural funds was made. Town Manager’s Report, John Anzivino, Interim Town Manager  Interim Town Manager John Anzivino reported on staff meetings, current projects, Harvest Festival preparations, a fiscal-impact analysis for a proposed subdivision in the Route 301 corridor project, anticipated zoning updates, and FY2026 audit preparations. He noted the need to complete financial reconciliations, develop cash-flow and capital-project funding plans, and coordinate a CivicPlus website update. He also presented a Virginia Foundation for Healthy Youth grant opportunity for playground matting, with awards up to $100,000, no local match, and reimbursement of eligible expenditures. The application deadline was October 28, and funds would need to be expended by July 15, 2027. Staff would determine the matting cost and provide a subsequent update. Councilmember Randy Hageman reported potential REC volunteer assistance for the playground installation, and staff emphasized volunteer registration. 4 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 3 of 5  Councilmember Randy Hageman moved to authorize staff to pursue grant funding for playground matting. The motion was seconded by Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle and carried unanimously by roll-call vote, with six affirmative votes and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. UNFINISHED BUSINESS: 7. Proposed Replacement of Article 4.10 — Parking Regulations  Council reviewed the proposed ordinance and discussed discrepancies between the summary and ordinance concerning large commercial vehicles, school buses, and recreational vehicles. Town Attorney Jeff Gore explained that the overnight parking provision addressed street parking and that the summary appeared to retain language from an earlier draft. Council also discussed fire-lane markings and the previously identified Lakewood Road correction. Staff reported receipt of VDOT comments concerning golf carts and was asked to follow up on fire-lane issues with VDOT and the fire department.  Councilmember David Storke moved to approve the parking ordinance as amended. The motion was seconded by Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle and carried unanimously by roll-call vote, with six affirmative votes and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. NEW BUSINESS: 8. Referral of Cannabis Regulations to the Planning Commission  Deputy Zoning Administrator Darla Odom presented the proposed approach to cannabis-related zoning regulations. She described the state licensing framework and the need to prepare local regulations addressing definitions, zoning districts, approval requirements, separation distances, hours, signage, odor control, security, parking, and enclosed operations. Council discussed available local authority, potential tax provisions, and consideration of practices in other jurisdictions. Council encouraged timely preparation of appropriate regulations without unnecessary complexity.  Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle moved that Town Council initiate a zoning text amendment to regulate cannabis businesses and refer the matter to the Planning Commission for consideration and a public hearing at its November 2026 meeting, with the Commission’s recommendation returned to Town Council. The motion was seconded by Councilmember David Storke and carried unanimously by roll-call vote, with six affirmative votes and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. 9. Caroline Historical Society Request for Courthouse Lane Building for Storage Assistance  Caroline Historical Society President Kathy McVey requested assistance with storage, including possible donation or lease of the Town-owned Courthouse Lane building with utility costs also donated by the Town. She explained that the Society currently paid $130.50 monthly for storage and a new structure, as proposed, would also welcome space for art shows and sales. Council discussed reported the structures mold and moisture issues, possible remediation costs, liability, the original property transfer, and potential future Town staffing and records-storage needs. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino recommended assessing the building’s condition, potential uses, and improvement costs before deciding its disposition. A limited storage lease and placement of a separate storage building on Town property were discussed as possible alternatives. Council requested further investigation, including review of available inspection and repair information, before responding. No donation or lease was approved. 10. Request to Waive Town Hall Rental Fees for Bowling Green Fire Department Event  Council considered a request to waive Town Hall rental fees for the Bowling Green Fire Department’s October 3 fundraising dinner, with setup October 2. The event was expected to draw approximately 300 attendees. The fee waiver was presented as approximately $1,300. Council requested documentation of the department’s nonprofit status for Town records.  Councilmember David Storke moved to waive the rental fee. The motion was seconded by Councilmember Randy Hageman and carried by roll-call vote with five affirmative votes, Councilmember Jeff Voit abstaining, and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. 5 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 4 of 5 INFORMATIONAL ITEMS: 11. DOJ Web Access Ruling: WCAG 2.1 AA Requirements  Administrative Assistant/Deputy Clerk Jeffrey Smith provided an update on website accessibility planning and reported an April 26, 2028, compliance deadline. He noted that 374 of the 375 PDFs reviewed in the Town’s website compliance report had accessibility issues and were out of compliance with federal requirements. Staff was continuing to evaluate compliance options, including CivicPlus DocAccess, for which the first-year quote was $4,297. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino advised that associated costs should be considered in the FY2028 budget. Further information would be provided during the upcoming budget cycle. No action was requested or taken. PUBLIC COMMENTS: 3 MINUTES PER INDIVIDUAL  Mayor Tina Gambill did not reopen public comment because no members of the public remained to speak. MEMBER COMMENTS:  Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle raised concerns about the possible removal of the UPS drop box and uncertainty regarding local package drop-off options. Staff agreed to investigate and provide clarification for residents.  Councilmember David Storke emphasized maintaining momentum in the Town’s intergovernmental support agreement with Fort A.P. Hill and exploring increased project limits and administrative revenue. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino reported that staff remained engaged with Fort A.P. Hill and would follow up on opportunities to expand the program. Mayor Tina Gambill recognized the partnership’s accomplishments and national award nomination.  Councilmember Randy Hageman welcomed Interim Town Manager John Anzivino and asked about FOIA and conflict-of-interest training. Mayor Tina Gambill suggested coordinated attendance at the January Virginia Municipal League newly elected officials conference. Town Attorney Jeff Gore discussed available training resources. Councilmember Randy Hageman also requested review of vehicle-repair activities, outdoor conditions, and compliance with prior approvals at the North Main Street automobile dealership.  Mayor Tina Gambill raised business concerns about the fats, oils, and grease program. Councilmember Randy Hageman relayed information from Mark Inboden concerning possible indoor grease traps and accommodations for existing businesses, with inspections and some improvements still anticipated. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino explained the program’s connection to wastewater permitting requirements. No ordinance amendment or exemption was adopted. 13. Proposal for Services  Councilmember David Storke presented a proposal from former Town Manager India Adams-Jacobs for possible transition and consulting services. Council discussed the scope, potential limitations associated with her employment elsewhere, and assistance with recruitment of a permanent Town Manager. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino recommended expanding the vacancy advertisement beyond the existing outlets to professional associations and recruitment sites in Virginia and neighboring states before deciding whether to engage an executive-search firm. Staff was directed to share the existing advertisement and broaden recruitment efforts. No consulting agreement or recruitment-firm engagement was approved. ADJOURNMENT: 12. Joint Town Council-Planning Commission Meeting and Public Hearing- October 22, 2026  Councilmember Jeff Voit motioned to recess the meeting until October 22, 2026, at 6:00 PM at Town Hall for the joint Town Council-Planning Commission meeting and public hearing. The motion was seconded by Councilmember Randy Hageman and carried unanimously by voice vote, with six members present and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. 6 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 5 of 5 Attest: Mayor: ___ Tina Gambill Clerk: ___ John Anzivino, Interim Town Manager/Clerk Attachments Referenced During Meeting: 7 Town Council Memorandum TO: FROM: SUBJECT: DATE: The Honorable Mayor and Town Council Chief J.O.Cecil Bowling Green Police Dept. Officers responded to a total of 54 calls for service and conducted numerous proactive patrols and preventative activities throughout the community. Activity during this reporting period included: • • • • • • • • 47 total calls for service 12 assists to other law enforcement and emergency service agencies 1 Motor Vehicle Accident 1 Domestic / Assault 22 traffic summonses issued 26 traffic warnings issued 64 property, vacation, and business security checks 3 Town Hall Events In addition to responding to calls for service, officers continued to emphasize proactive policing through regular property, vacation, and business checks to help deter criminal activity and provide reassurance to residents and business owners. Traffic enforcement efforts remained a priority as well.
